discovery: Quantum error correction and the theory of fault-tolerant quantum computation
motivation: Fragile quantum superpositions were long thought impossible to protect from decoherence, because measuring an error seemed to destroy the information. In 1995-96 Shor and Steane independently found quantum error-correcting codes that encode one logical qubit nonlocally across many physical qubits. Syndrome measurements then detect and reverse errors without learning the encoded state. Kitaev showed that topological order, as in the toric and surface codes, gives intrinsic protection, and he helped establish that arbitrarily long computations become possible once physical error rates fall below a threshold. This insight connects quantum mechanics, many-body physics and information theory. It now underpins every serious quantum-computing architecture. In 2024, experiments with superconducting processors showed logical errors falling exponentially as surface-code size increased below threshold, confirming the theory in the laboratory. Building on the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum circuits, this work turned quantum hardware into a scalable instrument for physics.
